paper_a_title: Making Retrieval-Augmented Language Models Robust to Irrelevant Context
paper_b_title: Enhancing Noise Robustness of Retrieval-Augmented Language Models with Adaptive Adversarial Training
what_valid_comparison_requires: same retriever/generator, negative type, rank position, gold-evidence availability, metric family, and explicit action policy
external_gold_rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RALMs on open-domain QA, share answer correctness (EM/F1) as the headline metric, overlap on NQ (and partially on TriviaQA/WebQ), and both include a generator-side training mitigation; RAAT even cites Yoran et al. as direct prior work. However, the noise scope diverges: Paper A confines failures to naturally retrieved irrelevant passages (benign retrieval error), while Paper B explicitly enlarges the taxonomy to include counterfactual passages — a consistency/conflict failure mode constructed as a benchmark stressor that Paper A never evaluates. The intervention surfaces are asymmetric (NLI filter at context-assembly stage plus fine-tuning vs. adversarial training plus an auxiliary noise classifier with no filtering stage), and the effective action policies differ (filter-then-answer with a no-retrieval fallback vs. always-answer). A leaderboard-style ranking would therefore conflate a filter+train pipeline operating on naturally noisy retrieval with an adversarially trained generator operating on a synthesized three-way noise mixture; the works are best framed as complementary mechanisms covering overlapping but non-identical operating regions, which is the canonical 'partial' case.
external_gold_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the retriever (e.g., DPR over Wikipedia with the same top-k), the generator backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), and the training-data budget; evaluate both methods on a unified noise protocol that explicitly partitions irrelevant vs. counterfactual (and ideally relevant-but-distracting) subsets with matched injection rates, reporting EM/F1 per noise slice on a shared dataset (at minimum NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ, plus a multi-hop slice to respect Paper A's scope). Harmonize the action policy by either (a) ablating Paper A's NLI filter so both systems are answer-only, or (b) adding a comparable filter/abstain wrapper to RAAT, and report selective-risk/coverage curves alongside accuracy so the filter action is not silently credited. Ideally, cross-apply each intervention (NLI filter stacked on a RAAT-trained generator, and RAAT training evaluated on Paper A's multi-hop benchmarks) so the contribution of each intervention point is isolated rather than confounded with method identity.
external_gold_disagreement_summary: Unanimous consensus: 30/30 annotators returned 'partial' at confidence 4. There was no split on the verdict. Minor variation appeared only in how the breaking coordinates were emphasized — most cited all four (failure_type, evidence_assumption, intervention_point, action_policy), a few highlighted only three, and one framed the action policy as 'unreported' rather than divergent — but the underlying reasoning (broader noise taxonomy in B, filter-vs-training asymmetry, mismatched action policies, complementary rather than substitutable methods) was identical. 'Partial' was selected because the papers clearly share problem family and metric but diverge on multiple comparability coordinates in ways that block direct ranking.

paper_a_title: Making Retrieval-Augmented Language Models Robust to Irrelevant Context
paper_b_title: Benchmarking Large Language Models in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
what_valid_comparison_requires: same benchmark item set, same evidence state, same metric family, and explicit answer/abstain policy
external_gold_rationale: Both papers concern RAG behavior under noisy or irrelevant retrieved evidence, so the relevance/noise failure type genuinely overlaps. However, irrelevantContext2023 is a method paper that intervenes at context assembly (NLI filtering) and at the generator (mixed-context fine-tuning) and reports answer-correctness on five ODQA benchmarks under naturally retrieved noise, while rgb2023 is a diagnostic benchmark (RGB) that constructs four orthogonal testbeds — noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness — with controlled noise ratios and synthetic counterfactuals, and crucially scores abstention as a first-class outcome. The intervention point (mitigation vs. evaluation artifact), evidence construction (organic retriever errors vs. engineered stressors), action policy (filter+answer vs. answer+abstain), and metric family (single QA accuracy vs. multi-ability with selective risk) all diverge. They are therefore complementary — Paper A's methods could be scored on Paper B's benchmark — rather than substitutable entries on the same leaderboard, which makes the comparison partial rather than valid or invalid.
external_gold_valid_comparison_requires: Run irrelevantContext2023's NLI-filter and robust fine-tuned generator on rgb2023's four RGB testbeds (especially noise robustness and negative rejection, ideally also counterfactual robustness) using the same base LLM backbones, same retriever or supplied document sets, and matched noise-ratio buckets; jointly report answer accuracy AND an explicit rejection/abstention rate under a single declared action-policy schema (answer vs. abstain vs. filter). Symmetrically, evaluate the LLMs studied in rgb2023 on the five ODQA benchmarks from irrelevantContext2023 with the same retriever, top-k, prompt, and action labels. Without aligned retriever/corpus, harmonized noise construction, a shared metric family covering both correctness and selective risk, and matched action-policy reporting, leaderboard-style ranking is not meaningful.
external_gold_disagreement_summary: Unanimous: all 30 independent adjudicators returned 'partial' at confidence 4. There was no split on the label; minor variation appeared only in which coordinate was emphasized as most decisive (method-vs-benchmark asymmetry at the intervention coordinate, vs. the missing abstention/selective-risk action policy in Paper A). The final label reflects the convergent reasoning that the noise-robustness construct is shared but the contribution types and evaluated action sets are not substitutable.

paper_a_title: Enhancing Noise Robustness of Retrieval-Augmented Language Models with Adaptive Adversarial Training
paper_b_title: Benchmarking Large Language Models in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
what_valid_comparison_requires: training and benchmark results on the same model, noise construction, and ability-specific metric
external_gold_rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RAG and share overlapping noise typologies — irrelevant and counterfactual/misleading retrieved passages — so the failure-type and benchmark-stressor coordinates genuinely overlap. However, RAAT is a training-time intervention on the generator (adaptive adversarial fine-tuning of LLaMA-2 7B with a noise-aware multi-task head) evaluated only with F1/EM on its own RAG-Bench under an answer-only action policy, while RGB is purely a diagnostic evaluation artifact that decomposes RAG into four separately scored abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) over bilingual news data across six off-the-shelf LLMs and explicitly measures abstention. Because the intervention points differ categorically (method vs. benchmark), the action-policy spaces differ in a load-bearing way (RGB rewards correct abstention; RAAT never reports a coverage/risk tradeoff), and the metric families and corpora diverge, the two cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as substitutable approaches. They are instead clearly complementary — RAAT is a candidate method that could in principle be scored on RGB — which is precisely the partial regime rather than valid or invalid.
external_gold_valid_comparison_requires: Run the RAAT-trained LLaMA-2 7B (plus a non-RAAT baseline of the same backbone) on all four RGB testbeds in both English and Chinese, reporting RGB's full metric suite (accuracy, rejection rate, error-detection rate, error-correction rate) under matched noise-ratio sweeps; conversely, evaluate the LLMs benchmarked by RGB on RAAT's RAG-Bench with the same DPR retriever and identical relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual noise splits. The comparison further requires aligning the retriever, generator family, corpus, noise-construction protocol, language coverage, and — most importantly — an explicit action-policy specification (answer vs. abstain vs. expose conflict) so that selective-risk behavior is measured on both sides rather than implicitly fixed to answer-always.
external_gold_disagreement_summary: No disagreement: all 30 independent adjudicators returned partial with confidence 4, and converged on the same dominant breaks — intervention_point (training method vs. evaluation artifact) and action_policy (answer-only vs. answer+abstain via negative rejection), with metric_target as a secondary break. A small minority additionally flagged evidence_assumption (different corpora and noise-construction pipelines) as breaking; the panel includes this as a contributing factor in the rationale but treats the three coordinates above as the load-bearing breaks. Partial was preferred over under-specified because the coordinate mismatches are clearly identifiable from the published artifacts, and over invalid because the problem framing and noise typology genuinely overlap and one paper could in principle be scored on the other's harness.

paper_a_title: Chain-of-Note: Enhancing Robustness in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
paper_b_title: Making Retrieval-Augmented Language Models Robust to Irrelevant Context
what_valid_comparison_requires: same retrieved contexts and generator with both context filtering and generator-reasoning interventions compared under the same action policy
external_gold_rationale: Both papers target the same failure mode — RALM distraction by irrelevant retrieved context in open-domain QA under benign retrieval error — and share answer-correctness reporting on overlapping benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA), so they are clearly in the same problem family. However, the intervention points diverge: Chain-of-Note rewires generator reasoning via per-document notes, while Yoran et al. intervene upstream with an NLI passage filter and additionally fine-tune on mixed-quality contexts (with explicit multi-hop emphasis that CoN does not test). Crucially, the action policies are different first-class behaviors — CoN explicitly evaluates abstention ('unknown') and reports rejection rate as a selective-risk metric, whereas Yoran et al. operate filter-then-answer with no abstention metric. Because a single leaderboard EM number would conflate a coverage-trading abstainer with an evidence-pruning answerer, and because the two mechanisms could in principle be stacked (NLI filter → CoN reader → abstain), they are best framed as complementary modules at different pipeline stages and different operating regions, not as substitutable methods.
external_gold_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the same retriever (e.g., DPR top-k from the same Wikipedia dump) and the same base generator (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B); evaluate on a shared benchmark suite covering single-hop ODQA (NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ), multi-hop QA (e.g., StrategyQA/2WikiMultiHopQA), and an unanswerable/real-time slice; impose a common action-policy contract where both systems are evaluated under matched options (answer-only, answer+abstain, answer+filter+abstain); report a unified metric bundle including EM/F1, abstention/rejection rate, accuracy-on-answered (selective risk), risk-coverage curves, and accuracy delta vs. no-retrieval baseline; include ablations that (a) pipeline NLI filtering before CoN to disentangle filter-stage from generator-stage gains, (b) disable CoN's abstain head to isolate the note-taking contribution, and (c) add an abstain head to the Yoran fine-tune so action policies are commensurate; match training-data budgets and noise-injection protocols across the two systems.
external_gold_disagreement_summary: Unanimous: all 30 independent adjudicators returned 'partial' at confidence 4. There was no split on verdict. Annotators consistently identified the same three breaking coordinates (action_policy, intervention_point, metric_target) and the same underlying logic: shared failure type and benign-retrieval assumption, but asymmetric abstention behavior and different intervention loci make leaderboard-style ranking misleading. Several reviewers emphasized that this is genuinely 'partial' rather than 'under-specified' because both papers do explicitly declare their action policies (abstain vs. filter) — the gap is real divergence, not missing information.

paper_a_title: Sufficient Context: A New Lens on Retrieval Augmented Generation Systems
paper_b_title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
what_valid_comparison_requires: fixed evidence-sufficiency labels and the same action set: answer, abstain, retrieve, or critique
external_gold_rationale: Both papers target RAG reliability when retrieved evidence is irrelevant or insufficient, and both add a self-assessment signal to govern generation behavior, so the failure-type axis (sufficiency / relevance noise) and the benign-retrieval evidence assumption overlap. However, Sufficient Context is an inference-time selective-generation method that uses an external (Q,C) autorater plus self-confidence to drive an explicit answer-vs-abstain policy, scored primarily via selective-risk/coverage curves and correctness-conditional-on-answering. Self-RAG instead retrains the generator end-to-end with reflection tokens that drive on-demand re-retrieval, passage filtering, and citation-grounded self-critique, with headline metrics on factuality and citation accuracy for long-form generation. The intervention point (post-hoc verifier+policy wrapper vs. training-time integrated reflective LM with adaptive retriever), the explicit action policy (abstain vs. re-retrieve/filter/answer-with-critique), and the dominant metric family (selective risk vs. citation faithfulness) all diverge enough that direct leaderboard ranking would conflate orthogonal mechanisms. They are best framed as complementary modules in a robust-RAG stack rather than substitutable systems on a single leaderboard.
external_gold_valid_comparison_requires: Hold retriever, corpus, and base generator backbone fixed; evaluate both methods on a shared benchmark suite spanning short-form QA and long-form attribution-evaluable tasks; report a common metric bundle covering (a) selective accuracy / coverage-risk curves with an explicit abstain action, (b) hallucination rate at matched coverage, (c) citation precision/recall and evidence support, and (d) retrieval cost/latency. Both systems must expose the same action-policy taxonomy (answer / abstain / re-retrieve), with Self-RAG's reflection tokens operationalized into an abstain rule (e.g., via ISREL/ISSUP thresholds) and Sufficient Context wrapped with an optional re-retrieve branch. Ideally add ablations where the sufficiency autorater is stacked on top of a Self-RAG generator to isolate the contribution of inference-time gating vs. training-time reflection.
external_gold_disagreement_summary: No disagreement: all 30 independent adjudicators returned 'partial' at confidence 4, with highly convergent rationales centered on mismatched intervention point (inference-time selective wrapper vs. trained reflective LM), mismatched explicit action policy (abstain vs. re-retrieve/filter), and only partially overlapping metric families (selective risk vs. citation faithfulness). The panel adopts this consensus verdict and rationale.

paper_b_title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
what_valid_comparison_requires: same confidence target, coverage/risk metric, retrieval cost, and action set
external_gold_rationale: Both papers fall under the broad 'control / reliability of RAG' umbrella under a benign retrieval assumption, but they target different failure modes with different control surfaces. CalibRAG attacks miscalibration of decision confidence by training a forecasting function over (temperature, query, document) that reranks documents and exposes a calibrated probability, with calibration error as the headline metric. Self-RAG attacks indiscriminate retrieval and unsupported generation by training the generator to emit reflection tokens that drive on-demand retrieval and self-critique, with factuality and citation faithfulness as headline metrics. The intervention points (reranker/forecaster vs. generator training plus retrieval gate), primary metric families (calibration vs. citation/factuality), and action policies (calibrated answer vs. adaptive retrieve/critique) all diverge, so a leaderboard-style ranking would conflate calibration quality with adaptive-retrieval and grounding quality. They are best framed as complementary modules in a reliability stack rather than substitutable methods, which is why partial rather than valid or invalid is appropriate; the information needed to judge is present in both papers, so under-specified is not warranted.
external_gold_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation suite that (1) fixes the same retriever, generator backbone, and corpus; (2) reports a common metric battery covering both calibration (ECE/Brier, selective risk/coverage) AND factuality/citation faithfulness (e.g., FActScore, citation precision/recall) AND answer correctness on the same outputs; (3) specifies and evaluates an explicit, matched action policy (e.g., answer vs. abstain at a shared confidence threshold and/or re-retrieve under a common budget) so both systems are scored on the same decision interface; and (4) ideally cross-applies each mechanism to the other's primary metric (Self-RAG calibrated via something like CalibRAG; CalibRAG augmented with on-demand retrieval) so contributions can be disentangled rather than ranked head-to-head.
external_gold_disagreement_summary: Unanimous: 30/30 adjudicators independently chose 'partial' with confidence 4, with highly consistent five-coordinate codings (failure type, intervention point, metric target, and action policy all flagged as breaking; benign retrieval evidence assumption shared). No dissent on label or rationale structure, so 'partial' at confidence 4 is the natural panel verdict.

paper_a_title: FaithfulRAG: Fact-Level Conflict Modeling for Context-Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
what_valid_comparison_requires: same threat class and objective, or separate conflict detection from adversarial steering
external_gold_rationale: Both papers touch the broad theme that retrieved context can drive an LLM toward an answer that diverges from its parametric prior, but that surface overlap is the only thing they share. FaithfulRAG is a generator-side defense for naturally occurring parametric-vs-context knowledge conflicts, evaluated on answer correctness and faithfulness with no adversary in the loop. PoisonedRAG is an offensive corpus-poisoning attack that assumes an adversary with write access to the knowledge base, attacker-chosen target questions/answers, and a ~5-passage insertion budget, and is scored by attack success rate; it proposes no defender action policy. All five coordinates diverge — failure type (benign conflict vs. adversarial corruption), evidence assumption (natural vs. attacker-created), intervention point (generator vs. corpus), metric target (correctness vs. ASR), and action policy (answer-with-reconciliation vs. none) — and the artifacts play categorically opposite roles (defense vs. attack). A leaderboard-style ranking would conflate an attack benchmark with a non-adversarial faithfulness method and would mislead readers, so the comparison is invalid rather than merely partial.
external_gold_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe as an attack-vs-defense joint evaluation rather than leaderboard substitution: (1) instantiate PoisonedRAG as the attack with a fixed threat model (same corpus, retriever, generator, target-question set, ~5-text insertion budget, black/white-box variants); (2) evaluate FaithfulRAG (and matched baselines such as perplexity filtering, paraphrasing, majority voting) as candidate defenses under that threat model; (3) report a shared metric family — ASR / target-answer rate, clean-task accuracy, accuracy-under-attack, and ideally selective risk/coverage — on the same benchmarks; and (4) declare an explicit defender action policy (answer / abstain / expose-conflict / quarantine / re-retrieve) measured consistently across both systems. Only under this matched threat-model and metric protocol can the two works be meaningfully co-located, and even then as defense-vs-attack, not as substitutable robust-RAG methods.
external_gold_disagreement_summary: No disagreement: all 30 independent adjudicators returned 'invalid', 28/30 at confidence 5 and 2/30 at confidence 4. The shared reasoning is the attack-vs-defense category mismatch and divergence on every one of the five coordinates. The panel adopts 'invalid' with full confidence; the only minor variation across annotators was whether to additionally tag 'evaluation artifact' as an intervention point for PoisonedRAG, which does not affect the verdict.

paper_a_title: Astute RAG: Overcoming Imperfect Retrieval Augmentation and Knowledge Conflicts for Large Language Models
paper_b_title: PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
what_valid_comparison_requires: same source of contradiction, attacker capability, metric target, and required action
external_gold_rationale: Both papers sit in the broader robust/secure-RAG space and Astute RAG explicitly cites PoisonedRAG when motivating malicious retrieval, but they occupy fundamentally opposite roles in the attack-defense pipeline and cannot be placed on a common leaderboard as substitutable methods. PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution that intervenes at the corpus/index by injecting ~5 optimization-crafted malicious passages per target question under an explicit threat model and reports attack success rate, while Astute RAG is a defensive, training-free generator-side method that consolidates internal and external knowledge and reports answer correctness under noisy/conflicting (mostly benchmark-constructed) retrieval. The intervention points (corpus injection vs generator consolidation), metric targets (ASR vs accuracy — with inverted polarities), evidence assumptions (attacker-created with corpus write access vs benign/benchmark noise and conflict), and action policies (none vs answer-after-reliability-selection) all diverge, and neither paper evaluates the other's setting: Astute RAG is never tested against PoisonedRAG-style optimized injections, and PoisonedRAG does not include Astute RAG among its defenses. A direct leaderboard-style ranking would be a category error that conflates threat creation with threat mitigation.
external_gold_breaking_coordinates: role asymmetry (attack vs defense), intervention_point, metric_target, evidence_assumption (threat model), action_policy
external_gold_valid_comparison_requires: Recast both works inside a shared attack-vs-defense evaluation harness: fix the retriever, generator, corpus, and target-question set; instantiate PoisonedRAG (both black-box and white-box variants) as the adversary with matched insertion budgets (e.g., 1/3/5/10 malicious texts per target); evaluate Astute RAG alongside other defenses (e.g., RobustRAG, paraphrase/perplexity filtering, conflict-aware decoding) on the resulting poisoned corpora; report a joint metric suite covering attack success rate, clean-task accuracy, accuracy-under-attack, abstention/coverage, and any verify/quarantine action policy. Only then can defenses be ranked head-to-head under a common threat model, and even then PoisonedRAG belongs on a different axis (stressor/benchmark) rather than as a peer method to Astute RAG.
external_gold_disagreement_summary: 23 of 30 adjudicators voted invalid and 7 voted partial. Both camps identified essentially the same five-coordinate breaks (intervention point, metric target, evidence assumption, action policy, attack-vs-defense role), so the split is purely about how to label that asymmetry. The partial minority emphasized the shared corruption-integrity surface and Astute RAG's motivational citation of PoisonedRAG, treating the pair as complementary modules. The invalid majority — at higher average confidence (mostly 4-5) — emphasized inverted metric polarities (ASR vs accuracy), opposite pipeline-stage interventions, and the absence of any shared experimental harness, arguing that leaderboard-style ranking would be a category error rather than partial overlap. The panel sided with the majority because the metric inversion alone makes the two artifacts non-substitutable on any common axis.

paper_a_title: PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
paper_b_title: Certifiably Robust RAG against Retrieval Corruption
what_valid_comparison_requires: aligned corruption budget, corpus access, retrieval success, generator access, clean utility, and defense action
external_gold_rationale: Both papers operate in the same threat space — integrity/adversarial corruption of RAG via attacker-injected passages with corpus write access and a bounded insertion budget — so failure type and evidence assumption are cleanly aligned. However, PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution whose intervention is corpus-side injection and whose metric is attack success rate with no defender action policy, while RobustRAG is a defensive contribution whose intervention is isolate-then-aggregate at context assembly and generator prompting, with metrics on certified answer correctness and an explicit abstain action. The two artifacts occupy opposite roles within the same threat model: one maximizes ASR, the other maximizes certified accuracy under bounded corruption, and ranking them on a single leaderboard would be category-confused. They are naturally complementary — RobustRAG should be stress-tested against PoisonedRAG-style attacks — which matches the rulebook's definition of partial (complementary modules with non-fatal differences in intervention, metric, and action) rather than invalid (incompatible problem settings).
external_gold_breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, role (attacker artifact vs defender artifact)
external_gold_valid_comparison_requires: Direct head-to-head leaderboard ranking is structurally inappropriate because attack and defense play different roles. Comparability should be reframed as a shared attack-defense evaluation harness: fix retriever, generator, corpus, target-query distribution, and insertion budget m; instantiate PoisonedRAG (black-box and white-box, plus adaptive variants aware of isolate-then-aggregate) as the adversary; report RobustRAG's certified accuracy, empirical robust accuracy, clean accuracy, abstention rate, and ASR under attack, alongside an undefended baseline and at least one alternative defense. Alternatively, restrict ranking to role-homogeneous leaderboards: PoisonedRAG vs other corpus-poisoning attacks (Phantom, GASLITE, GCG-text) under a fixed defense on ASR with stealth/quality metrics, or RobustRAG vs other defenses (perplexity filtering, majority voting, paraphrasing) under a fixed PoisonedRAG attack on certified/empirical robust accuracy with matched k'. Explicit action-policy labels (answer/abstain/filter) must be reported on both sides.
external_gold_disagreement_summary: 22/30 adjudicators voted partial and 8/30 voted invalid; no votes for valid or under-specified. Both camps converged on the same structural diagnosis (shared failure type and evidence assumption, opposite attack-vs-defense roles, mismatched intervention/metric/action coordinates) but split on whether the role asymmetry is non-fatal (partial) or category-incoherent (invalid). The panel resolved in favor of partial because (a) the rulebook explicitly reserves partial for 'complementary modules' with non-fatal differences in intervention/metric/action, which precisely describes attack-defense pairings within a shared threat model; (b) the two papers' threat-model parameters (corpus write access, bounded insertion budget, adaptive/targeted attacker) are coherent enough that joint co-evaluation is natural and routine in the literature; and (c) reserving 'invalid' for genuinely incompatible problem settings (e.g., different failure types or assumption families) preserves discriminating power.

paper_a_title: RAGTruth: A Hallucination Corpus for Developing Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
paper_b_title: Benchmarking Large Language Models in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
what_valid_comparison_requires: same system outputs scored with both answer correctness and claim-level support, with a rule for unsupported correct answers
external_gold_rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation artifacts concerned with trustworthy generation under retrieved evidence, and they overlap on consistency/conflict failures (RAGTruth's evident-conflict spans, RGB's counterfactual robustness). However, RAGTruth is a span-annotated corpus over naturally generated LLM responses whose primary scored object is a hallucination detector (verify action, span-level faithfulness metric), while RGB is a constructed-stressor multi-ability testbed that scores end-to-end generator behavior on answer accuracy and explicit abstention. Because the evidence-construction regime (natural vs. injected), the metric family (detector span-F1 vs. ability-specific accuracy/rejection rates), the unit of evaluation (span vs. case), and the action policy (none vs. answer/abstain/expose-conflict) all diverge, a number reported on one benchmark cannot be ranked against a number reported on the other. They are best framed as complementary diagnostics covering distinct slices of robust RAG (detector quality vs. generator capability profile), which makes partial the correct verdict rather than valid or invalid.
external_gold_breaking_coordinates: evidence_assumption, metric_target, action_policy (with secondary breaks in failure_type scope and granularity: span vs case)
external_gold_valid_comparison_requires: Align both benchmarks on (a) a shared evaluated object — either both score a hallucination detector or both score an end-to-end generator under the same action-policy contract; (b) a shared evidence-construction protocol with matched natural and constructed stressor conditions (e.g., apply RGB-style noise/counterfactual injections to RAGTruth contexts, or run RAGTruth-style word-level annotation on RGB outputs); (c) a unified metric family that jointly reports span-level faithfulness, end-task answer correctness, and abstention/coverage at matched thresholds; and (d) identical retriever and generator stacks so detector-quality gains and generator-robustness gains are separable. Without these, the two should be reported as complementary modules rather than leaderboard alternatives.
external_gold_disagreement_summary: All 30 independent adjudicators converged on 'partial' at confidence 4, with no dissent. The shared reasoning is that both works are surface-categorized as evaluation_benchmark and share a high-level robustness/faithfulness motivation, but they measure fundamentally different objects (verifier detection F1 over naturally generated spans vs. generator answer/abstain accuracy under constructed stressors). Minor variation appeared only in which secondary coordinate (intervention_point vs. failure_type scope) to list alongside the agreed core breaks; the final panel adopts evidence_assumption, metric_target, and action_policy as the primary breaks.

paper_a_title: Benchmarking Large Language Models in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: Sufficient Context: A New Lens on Retrieval Augmented Generation Systems
what_valid_comparison_requires: same items with evidence sufficiency labels, ability-specific metrics, and explicit answer/abstain policy
external_gold_rationale: Both papers study LLM behavior when retrieved context is imperfect and, unusually for this area, both explicitly treat answer-vs-abstain as a first-class action policy (RGB's 'negative rejection' and Sufficient Context's guided selective generation), so the failure-type and action-policy coordinates genuinely overlap. However, RGB is a pure diagnostic benchmark built from synthetically constructed stressors with four discrete ability testbeds (noise ratio sweeps, all-noise rejection, multi-document integration, counterfactual injection), reporting per-ability accuracy and rejection scores. Sufficient Context instead defines a (Q,C)-level sufficiency property, applies an LLM autorater to naturally retrieved contexts, and adds a verifier + selective-generation intervention scored with sufficiency-stratified correct/abstain/hallucinate rates and selective-risk curves. The evidence construction (constructed vs. autorater-labeled natural), intervention scope (eval-only vs. eval + verifier + generator policy), and metric framing (per-ability scores vs. selective risk-coverage) diverge enough that head-to-head leaderboard ranking would conflate a benchmark with an analysis-plus-method paper. They are best reported as complementary lenses on the same abstention problem, which is exactly the 'partial' verdict.
external_gold_valid_comparison_requires: Run Sufficient Context's sufficiency autorater and selective-generation policy on RGB's four testbeds (especially Negative Rejection and Noise Robustness) using the same backbone LLMs, retriever, prompts, and an explicit shared abstention threshold; conversely, apply RGB-style controlled noise-ratio and counterfactual injections to HotPotQA/Musique/FreshQA and re-stratify by the sufficiency autorater. Report a unified metric family — per-ability accuracy, abstention rate, hallucination rate, and selective risk-coverage curves — computed on identical (query, context, action-label) tuples so that RGB's 'negative rejection' and Sufficient Context's 'abstain when insufficient' are operationalized identically.
external_gold_disagreement_summary: Unanimous: 30/30 adjudicators chose 'partial' at confidence 4. All converged on the same three breaking coordinates (intervention_point, evidence_assumption, metric_target) and explicitly noted that action_policy is shared (both evaluate abstention), which is why the verdict is partial rather than under-specified. The only minor variation was whether to also list failure_type as a break given RGB's broader coverage (counterfactual/integration), but this was treated as a scope-overlap issue rather than a contradiction. paper_a_title: RAGTruth: A Hallucination Corpus for Developing Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
paper_b_title: FaithfulRAG: Fact-Level Conflict Modeling for Context-Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
what_valid_comparison_requires: same fact-level support labels, conflict cases, and citation/faithfulness metric target
external_gold_rationale: Both papers address faithfulness failures in RAG generation and share consistency/conflict as a core failure mode, since RAGTruth annotates 'Evident Conflict' spans and FaithfulRAG explicitly targets parametric-vs-retrieved knowledge conflict. However, they occupy categorically different roles in the pipeline: RAGTruth is an evaluation artifact (a word-level hallucination corpus across QA, data-to-text, and summarization, plus a fine-tuned detector baseline) measured by span-level detection F1, while FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention (self-fact mining, contextual alignment, self-think reconciliation) measured by end-task answer correctness on conflict QA. The intervention point (evaluation artifact + verifier vs. context assembly + generator prompting), metric family (detection F1 vs. answer correctness), action policy (verify/flag vs. answer-after-reconcile), and failure-type scope (broad hallucination taxonomy vs. narrow knowledge conflict) all diverge, so a single leaderboard ranking would conflate a measurement instrument with a generation method. The two artifacts are best framed as pipeline-complementary—FaithfulRAG outputs could in principle be scored by RAGTruth's annotation protocol—which fits the protocol's definition of partial (complementary modules / different operating regions) rather than invalid (incompatible assumptions).
external_gold_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) evaluate FaithfulRAG-generated outputs on the RAGTruth corpus (especially the QA and conflict subsets) using its span/response-level hallucination annotation protocol with matched retriever, generator backbone, prompt conditions, and report both span-level hallucination rate and end-task answer correctness; or (b) deploy a RAGTruth-fine-tuned detector as a runtime verifier with an explicit action policy (answer / abstain / flag / re-retrieve) on FaithfulRAG's conflict QA benchmarks under identical retriever, generator, and conflict construction. In both cases the systems must declare a common action policy and report a shared metric family (faithfulness/grounding plus answer correctness) so that detection-oriented and generation-oriented interventions become commensurate.
external_gold_disagreement_summary: 19/30 adjudicators voted partial and 11/30 voted invalid. Both camps identified essentially the same broken coordinates (intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, failure_type scope) and the same root cause: a benchmark/detector contribution paired with a generation-time conflict-resolution method. The invalid camp argued the category mismatch is severe enough that direct leaderboard ranking would be categorically misleading; the partial camp emphasized that the consistency/conflict failure-type overlap is genuine and the artifacts are naturally complementary (FaithfulRAG could be measured on RAGTruth-style annotations). The panel chose partial because the protocol's `partial` definition explicitly covers 'complementary modules / partial overlap' and reserves `invalid` for incompatible problem settings or assumptions, which is not the case here—both papers operate under the same benign-retrieval, faithfulness-failure regime.
